title: Lobbying

definition.text: Lobbying is legal advocacy that tries to influence decisions made by legislators, regulators or sometimes judges.

facts.text: Its main form is meeting lawmakers directly, armed with research, data and draft proposals.
Lobbyists can be individuals, corporations, nonprofits, interest groups and political action committees.
Inside lobbying deals with decision-makers directly; outside lobbying pressures them by mobilising public opinion.
Research documents three effects: trading money for access, persuading officials with information, and mobilising citizens or coalitions.
Lobbying can pull politicians away from the median voter, especially when special-interest money is high and public attention low.
It can encourage lax enforcement of laws and is seen as one cause of a democratic deficit.
Many governments require lobbyists to register and disclose spending, clients and issues.
A 2011 study found that firms spending most on lobbying relative to assets earned 'blistering' returns.

contested_note: The ethics of lobbying are disputed: it is defended as legitimate advocacy and attacked as corrupting the law for private interests.

definition.text: The fossil fuels lobby is the paid representatives of oil, gas and coal companies and related industries such as chemicals, plastics and aviation.

facts.text: Their wealth and economic importance give them the means to seek outsized influence on government policy.
The lobby promotes climate change denial and obstructs environmental and climate policy.
Lobbyists work to keep fossil fuel subsidies.
Fossil fuel interests spent $2 billion on climate-change lobbying in the US from 2000 to 2016, many times what citizens and environmentalists spent.
The five biggest oil and gas companies spent at least 251 million euros lobbying the EU on climate policy since 2010.
According to the UNFCCC, 636 fossil fuel lobbyists attended COP27.
In Canada, fossil fuel lobbyists contacted officials five times more than environmental groups between 2011 and 2018.
The lobby has used crises such as COVID-19 and the 2022 invasion of Ukraine to try to roll back regulations.

title: Median voter theorem

definition.text: The median voter theorem says that when voters and candidates line up along one left-right spectrum, majority-rule voting elects the candidate the middle (median) voter prefers.

facts.text: Voters are assumed to rank candidates by closeness; the candidate nearest the median voter then beats every rival by a majority.
Duncan Black first derived it in 1948, and Kenneth Arrow independently.
With two candidates a simple majority vote satisfies it; with more, any Condorcet method does.
In more than one dimension there may be no majority winner, as the McKelvey–Schofield chaos theorem shows.
It is popular in political economy because it yields testable links between voter characteristics and policy outcomes.
Levitt (1996) found senators from the same state but different parties voted only slightly more alike than random pairs, contradicting the theorem.

contested_note: Empirical studies from the US Senate and India find voting outcomes that contradict the theorem's predictions.

definition.text: The Hotelling–Downs model predicts that politicians who care only about winning will move to the median voter's position.

facts.text: It adapts Hotelling's 1929 principle of minimum differentiation in business competition, applied to politics by Anthony Downs in 1957.
In a two-party system it predicts both parties drift toward the median voter.
Primaries and most voting rules in national use break the conditions, so candidates may not converge.

title: Path dependence

definition.text: Path dependence is when past events or decisions constrain later ones, so that 'history matters' for where a system ends up.

facts.text: Economists developed it to explain how technologies are adopted and industries evolve.
A path-dependent process may settle into one of several equilibria depending on its starting point and chance events, unlike simple neoclassical models with one outcome.
Paul David argued in 1985 that a first-to-market standard such as the QWERTY keyboard can become entrenched even if inferior.
More than half the world's railways use the 143.5 cm standard gauge, inherited from early coal tramways.
Drivers include lock-in, positive feedback, increasing returns and self-reinforcement.
Commercial fisheries' harvest rates have been found to be path dependent, because institutions adapt slowly while ecosystems change fast.
Liebowitz and Margolis argue that inefficient lock-in is rare and that no real-world private cases exist.

contested_note: Economists still argue whether cases like QWERTY show real inefficient lock-in.

definition.text: A critical juncture is a moment when contingent choices set an institution on a path of development that is hard to reverse.

facts.text: Ruth and David Collier made the framework prominent in political science.
It has been used to explain the rise and persistence of welfare states and differences in economic development between countries.
Kathleen Thelen warns such frameworks are too deterministic, since institutions keep evolving.

definition.text: Regulatory capture is when a regulator or policymaker is co-opted to serve the interests of a small group, such as an industry, instead of the public.

facts.text: A special interest is then put ahead of the general public, causing a net loss for society.
Groups with high stakes focus resources on regulation, while the dispersed public, each with little at stake, does not.
George Stigler, a Nobel laureate economist, was a major developer of the theory.
A captured regulator can be worse than no regulation because it wields government authority; transparency may reduce the damage.
Smaller government units are easier for concentrated industries to capture, as with timber states blocking national policy.
The US Minerals Management Service was widely cited as captured after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill.
Water management in Australia's Murray–Darling Basin has been analysed as a case of rent-seeking and regulatory capture.

definition.text: Regulatory capture comes in two basic types: materialist (financial) capture driven by the regulator's self-interest, and non-materialist (cognitive) capture driven by biased views.

facts.text: Materialist capture can result from bribery, revolving doors, political donations or a regulator's wish to keep its funding.
Specialised technical industries risk cultural capture because regulators must hire experts who mostly come from the industry.
The top 5 financial companies account for around 80% of revolving-door movements, showing that big firms do most capturing.

definition.text: Rent-seeking is increasing one's wealth by manipulating public policy or economic conditions, without creating new wealth.

facts.text: It wastes resources, stifles competition, lowers wealth creation and government revenue, and raises inequality and corruption risk.
Robert Shiller's classic example is a landowner who chains a river and charges passing boats to lower the chain, adding no value.
Unlike profit-seeking, which creates wealth through mutually beneficial trade, rent-seeking redistributes existing wealth.
Here 'rent' means economic rent: income beyond what is needed to keep a factor in its current use.
Typical examples are lobbying for subsidies, tariffs, quotas or rules that hobble competitors.
Money spent on lobbyists rather than research or equipment slows economic growth.
Mancur Olson argued that countries dominated by organised interest groups lose vitality and decline.
Critics say it can be hard to tell beneficial profit-seeking from harmful rent-seeking.

definition.text: The Tullock paradox is the puzzle that rent-seekers can buy political favours for far less than the favours are worth to them.

facts.text: A rent-seeker hoping to gain a billion dollars may need to spend merely ten million, about 1% of the gain.
Proposed explanations include voters punishing lavish politicians, competition among politicians to offer favours, and lack of trust in illicit deals.

title: Logic of collective action

definition.text: Mancur Olson's 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action argues that small groups with concentrated interests win out over large groups with diffuse interests, because large groups suffer worse free-riding.

facts.text: Members of any group providing a public good are tempted to free ride on others' efforts.
Without selective incentives, collective action is unlikely even among large groups with shared interests.
Large groups face higher organising costs and each member gains less, so they are less able to act than small groups.
A minority bound by concentrated incentives can therefore dominate the majority.
Susanne Lohmann notes the US sugar import quota created 2,261 jobs while reducing overall welfare, and blames information asymmetry rather than free riding.
Gunnar Trumbull counters that diffuse interests such as consumers can win through a 'legitimacy premium' and coalitions.

contested_note: Lohmann, Trumbull, Marwell and Oliver, and Wilson each dispute parts of Olson's argument.

definition.text: Bootleggers and Baptists is Bruce Yandle's idea that regulations win support both from groups that want their stated purpose and from groups that profit from undermining it.

facts.text: The name comes from Sunday alcohol bans backed by Baptist activists and by bootleggers, who sold more when legal sales were restricted.
The 'Baptists' take the moral high ground and give politicians cover, while the 'bootleggers' lobby quietly behind closed doors.
It predicts that coalitions of opposing interests agreeing on one rule succeed more often than one-sided groups.
Such coalitions tend to produce suboptimal laws; a surtax on Sunday sales, for instance, could cut drinking as much as a ban.
Yandle and Buck applied it to the Kyoto Protocol: environmental groups gave moral support while corporations and nations sought advantage over rivals.
Smith and Yandle later distinguished covert, noncooperative, cooperative and coordinated patterns of interaction.
It has not been systematically validated empirically and is a useful catch-phrase rather than an accepted principle.

title: Network effect

definition.text: A network effect is when the value a user gets from a good or service depends on how many users of compatible products there are.

facts.text: Network effects are usually positive feedback systems: each added user raises the value for those already in the network.
Growth is not endless: a network tends to plateau at market saturation or when the cost of reaching the last customers becomes prohibitive.
A growing network effect does not always bring proportional returns; it depends on commoditization of supply, the type of added user and the substitutes available.
Network effects often yield multiple equilibria; expectations, shaped by path dependence such as first-mover advantage, decide which one appears and can produce lock-in.

notes: Seed page is mostly about technology markets; included for lock-in and path-dependence logic in technology adoption.

definition.text: Market tipping is the tendency of one system to pull away from its rivals in popularity once it has gained an initial edge.

facts.text: Tipping leaves one good or service dominant, stifles competition and can end in monopoly.
It happens because network effects give users an incentive to coordinate their adoption on a single product, a natural form of market concentration.

definition.text: Climate change denial is a form of science denial that rejects, disputes or fights the extensive evidence for human-caused global warming and the scientific consensus on it.

facts.text: Those promoting denial use rhetorical tactics to make a scientific controversy appear where none exists.
It includes raising unreasonable doubt about human causes and effects, and understating adaptation costs while overstating the costs of mitigation.
Its tactics include delaying mitigation, pushing adaptation only, disputing IPCC processes, and promoting conspiracy theories.
The downplaying approach was copied from tobacco lobbyists, who tried to prevent or delay regulation despite scientific evidence linking tobacco to lung cancer.

ExxonMobil led climate change denial from the 1980s to the mid 2000s and helped prevent US ratification of the Kyoto Protocol; research found its scientific opinion and public posture contradicted each other.
A 2008 University of Central Florida study found that 92% of environmentally skeptical literature published in the US was partly or wholly affiliated with conservative think tanks.
Denial campaigns have lowered public belief in climate change, which has affected legislative efforts to curb CO2 emissions.
As of February 2024, at least 32 US lawsuits sought damages from the fossil fuel industry for spreading denial despite knowing the risks.

definition.text: The psychology of climate change denial studies why people deny climate change despite the scientific consensus.

facts.text: One study identified seven psychological barriers to mitigation, adaptation and stewardship, including cognition, ideological worldviews, disbelief in experts, costs and perceived risks of change.
Climate denial is not simply overcome by reasoned argument, and supplying missing information or general science education may be ineffective.
Explaining techniques such as cherrypicking, fake experts and false balance has been shown to inoculate people somewhat against misinformation.

definition.text: Advocacy groups, also called lobby groups, interest groups or pressure groups, use advocacy or lobbying to influence political and social systems.

facts.text: Groups use lobbying, media campaigns, publicity stunts, polls, research and policy briefings to pursue their aims.
Some are backed by powerful business or political interests and exert considerable influence, while others have few resources; poorer groups may turn to direct action and civil disobedience.
In liberal democracies groups mainly work through the bureaucracy, where decision-making power lies, but access is generally limited to insiders such as large corporations and trade unions.
Groups with greater financial resources are generally better able to influence government decisions; large businesses gain from being key producers whose contributions matter to the economy.
Pluralism sees groups competing and acting as a counterweight to undue concentrations of power; neo-pluralism organises groups around a government department and its client groups.
Lobbying is regulated to stop the worst abuses, which can develop into corruption.

definition.text: Because members must be enticed to join an interest group, groups rely on a mix of free-rider-limiting benefits: selective, solidarity and expressive incentives.

facts.text: The free rider problem makes members hard to recruit when the benefits are enjoyed without joining; everyone gains from a cleaner environment, yet environmental groups do not get money from everyone.
Selective benefits are material rewards to members, such as discounted travel, meals or subscriptions.
Solidarity incentives are socially derived rewards of association, such as group identity and status.
Expressive incentives reward members for voicing a value they believe in whether or not the goal is achieved; environmental and public-interest groups rely on them.
